title: Tokyo 1964 gave Olympic sports a shared visual language
body: At the 1964 Olympics in Tokyo, designers standardised the little pictures used to identify sports and services. They reduced familiar actions to simple shapes that visitors could recognise across languages.
takeaway: The same approach works for wayfinding when readers have only a glance to find what they need.
source: International Olympic Committee, Olympic Games Marks
visual: a silhouetted runner clearing a hurdle against an empty stadium backdrop

title: On La Gomera, people can whistle Spanish sentences
body: Silbo Gomero encodes Spanish speech as whistles on the Canary Island of La Gomera. It uses two distinct whistle sounds to represent the five Spanish vowels and four for consonants. UNESCO listed the tradition in 2009.
takeaway: Listeners fill in distinctions from context, much as readers do when they make sense of a partly smudged word.
source: UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage, Silbo Gomero (2009)
visual: a distant figure signalling from a ridge above a deep ravine on La Gomera

title: The 1970 World Cup ball used 12 pentagons and 20 hexagons
body: The Telstar used in the 1970 FIFA World Cup was made from 32 hand-stitched leather panels. Its 12 pentagons were black and its 20 hexagons were white.
takeaway: The pentagons let the pattern close around a ball. Hexagons alone could spread across a flat surface.
source: Smithsonian National Museum of American History, Soccer Ball
visual: an unmarked stitched football on a dark patch of grass
